fullPassage: Until the camera came along to take photographs of living butterflies, the standard image of a butterfly was a grossly distorted one. It shows them not as they are in life but in death, mounted on a pin in a museum. The wings are held out flat at ninety degrees to the body — a posture which would sorely test the ligaments of any butterfly. It is nevertheless the shape which we instantly recognise as 'butterfly', whether in bow-ties or the pasta the Italians call farfalle (after farfalla, a butterfly). Yet in life butterflies open their wings flat only to enjoy the sun, and some species never do it at all, but settle with their wings tight shut. Even when the wings are wide open, they always slope downwards more than mounted specimens, with the hindwings much closer to the butterfly's body.
